title: Population Genetics: Hardy-Weinberg and Evolutionary Forces

generated.pipeline: extract → Sonnet draft → Sonnet accuracy gate (separate agent) → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: At a two-allele locus with alleles A and a, what do the allele frequencies p and q measure, and what do they sum to?
cards.back: p is the fraction of all allele copies that are A, and q the fraction that are a. With two alleles, p + q = 1.
cards.quote: the fraction of all allele copies that are A is p and the fraction that are a is q: the allele frequencies.
cards.section: The idea: with nothing acting, frequencies stay put

cards.front: State the one idea behind Hardy-Weinberg for a large population: what does mating do to allele frequencies, and what does dominance do?
cards.back: Mating reshuffles alleles, and dominance alone does not change their frequency.
cards.quote: Mating reshuffles alleles; dominance alone does not change their frequency.
cards.section: The idea: with nothing acting, frequencies stay put

cards.front: For a two-allele autosomal locus, give the Hardy-Weinberg genotype proportions and the baseline conditions they assume.
cards.back: AA = p^2, Aa = 2pq, aa = q^2. They assume a large population with random mating at the locus and no selection, mutation or migration.
cards.quote: The Hardy-Weinberg baseline below adds random mating at this locus and no selection, mutation or migration.
cards.section: The idea: with nothing acting, frequencies stay put

cards.front: A recessive allele a has frequency q = 0.10 in a population at Hardy-Weinberg proportions. What are the AA, Aa and aa genotype frequencies?
cards.quote: With an allele at 10%, only 1 person in 100 is aa, but 18 in 100 carry one copy.
cards.section: The idea: with nothing acting, frequencies stay put

cards.front: Show why one generation of random mating leaves the frequency of A unchanged at p.
cards.back: AA zygotes are all A and Aa zygotes half A, so A = p^2 + pq = p(p + q) = p, because p + q = 1.
cards.quote: p + q = 1, so this is just p.
cards.section: The idea: with nothing acting, frequencies stay put

cards.front: What role does the Hardy-Weinberg model play when we study real populations?
cards.back: It is a null model: the baseline expectation under the stated assumptions, against which departures are detected.
cards.quote: Hardy-Weinberg is a null model: what you would see under the baseline in the box above, against which you detect departures.
cards.section: The idea: with nothing acting, frequencies stay put

cards.front: At a codominant two-allele locus, 200 people are typed: AA 72, Aa 96, aa 32. What is the frequency of allele a?
cards.back: Count alleles, not people. a copies = 2 x 32 + 96 = 160 out of 400, so q = 0.40.
cards.quote: Count alleles, not people. Each MM person carries two M copies and each MN person one.

cards.front: When estimating allele frequencies from genotype counts, why count alleles first rather than take the square root of the homozygote frequency?
cards.back: The square-root shortcut assumes Hardy-Weinberg proportions. Counting alleles makes no such assumption, so the fit can be tested afterwards.
cards.quote: Count first; never find p from the square root of a homozygote frequency before you know the sample is at equilibrium.

cards.front: A sample of 200 people has allele frequency p = 0.7 for A at a two-allele locus. What genotype counts does Hardy-Weinberg expect?
cards.back: Multiply 200 by each proportion: AA = 200 x 0.49 = 98, Aa = 200 x 0.42 = 84, aa = 200 x 0.09 = 18.
cards.quote: Expected counts. Multiply the sample size by each Hardy-Weinberg proportion.

cards.front: A Hardy-Weinberg chi-square uses three genotype classes, with p estimated from the same sample. How many degrees of freedom, and why?
cards.back: One. Three classes, minus 1 because counts must add to the sample size, minus 1 because p was estimated from these counts.
cards.quote: Three classes, minus 1 because the counts must add to 1,000, minus 1 more because p was estimated from these same counts: 1, not 2.

cards.front: In a sample of 100, observed counts are AA 55, Aa 30, aa 15 and p = 0.7 was estimated from them. Test for Hardy-Weinberg at P = 0.05 (critical value 3.84).
cards.back: Expected 49, 42, 9. Chi-square = 36/49 + 144/42 + 36/9 = 0.73 + 3.43 + 4.00 = 8.16, above 3.84 on one degree of freedom. It departs, with too few heterozygotes.
cards.quote: The critical value at P = 0.05 for one degree of freedom is 3.84.

cards.front: A sample fits Hardy-Weinberg well. What does that fail to prove? A poor fit does not prove selection: name other causes.
cards.back: A good fit does not prove random mating or no selection. A poor fit can come from inbreeding, a sample mixing two populations, or genotyping errors.
cards.quote: a good fit does not prove random mating or the absence of selection, and a poor fit does not prove selection

cards.front: In a hypothetical population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, a recessive condition affects 1 in 40,000 newborns. About what fraction are carriers?
cards.quote: Affected people are aa, so q^2 = 1/2,500; the square root gives q = 1/50 = 0.02, and p = 0.98.

cards.front: Why does a rare recessive allele sit almost entirely in carriers rather than in affected people?
cards.back: Affected aa people are q^2, tiny for small q, while carriers are 2pq, about 2q. At q = 0.02, 98% of a copies are in carriers.
cards.quote: A rare allele sits almost entirely in heterozygotes: here 98% of a copies are in carriers.

cards.front: A child has a rare autosomal recessive condition, and no relative in the pedigree is affected. Is this surprising at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
cards.back: No. Almost every a copy is in an unaffected carrier, so both parents can be carriers with no affected relatives. Carriers are far commoner than affected people.
cards.quote: This is how families meet a recessive condition with no affected relatives in the pedigree.

cards.front: Name the two kinds of non-random mating.
cards.back: Inbreeding (mating between relatives) and assortative mating (partners alike in a trait the locus affects).
cards.quote: Its two kinds are inbreeding (mating between relatives) and assortative mating (partners alike in a trait the locus affects).

cards.front: Which of selection, drift, migration, mutation and non-random mating changes genotype frequencies without changing allele frequencies, and why?
cards.back: Non-random mating: same allele copies, different pairs. The other four can change allele frequencies.
cards.quote: Non-random mating is the odd one out, as the second film showed: same copies, different pairs.

cards.front: Why is selection against a rare recessive allele slow?
cards.back: Selection acts only on aa individuals, and almost every a copy is hidden in a carrier.
cards.quote: Against a rare recessive it is slow, because selection acts only on aa, and almost every a copy is hidden in a carrier.

cards.front: If aa individuals never reproduce, q_n = q_0 / (1 + n q_0). Starting at q_0 = 0.05, how many generations to halve q?
cards.back: Halving needs 1 + n x 0.05 = 2, so n = 20 generations.
cards.quote: Starting at 0.02, halving q to 0.01 takes 50 generations

cards.front: Residents have p = 0.3. Migrants have p = 0.7 and supply 20% of the copies. What is the new p?
cards.quote: The frequency moved a tenth of the way from 0.2 toward 0.6, because a tenth of the copies are new.

cards.front: Why is mutation weak at moving an allele frequency over a few generations?
cards.back: New changes are rare: about 1.2 x 10^-8 per base pair per generation in humans, so a few generations barely move a frequency.
cards.quote: estimated about 1.2 x 10^-8 new single-base changes per base pair per generation, a genome average

cards.front: What is genetic drift, and where does it end up if left long enough in a small population?
cards.back: Chance sampling of the parents' allele copies. The frequency wanders until the allele is lost (0) or fixed (1).
cards.quote: The second film's two cups showed drift: chance sampling of the parents' allele copies.
cards.section: Drift and founders: chance in small populations

cards.front: In the simplest drift model at constant Ne, is the one-generation variance of allele frequency larger at p = 0.5 or p = 0.1?
cards.back: Larger at p = 0.5, because p(1 - p) peaks halfway between the boundaries 0 and 1.
cards.quote: Larger at p = 0.5; p(1 - p) peaks halfway between the boundaries.
cards.section: Drift and founders: chance in small populations

cards.front: In the simplest drift model, one-generation variance is p(1 - p) / (2Ne). For Ne = 200 and p = 0.5, what is the standard deviation?
cards.back: Variance = 0.25 / 400 = 0.000625. The standard deviation is its square root, 0.025.
cards.quote: Across repeated populations, the one-generation changes have standard deviation 0.05.
cards.section: Drift and founders: chance in small populations

cards.front: Many replicate Drosophila populations, each kept at 8 males and 8 females, start an eye-colour allele at 0.5. After 19 generations, frequencies have spread apart, many lost or fixed it, but the mean stayed near 0.5. What does this show?
cards.back: Drift. Chance sampling in small populations pushes replicates in random directions, with no net change on average and some loss or fixation.
cards.quote: Over 19 generations they spread apart and many lost or fixed the allele, while their average stayed near where it began.
cards.section: Drift and founders: chance in small populations

cards.front: What is a founder effect?
cards.back: Drift at the start of a population: a small group carries, by chance, a different set of alleles than the population it left.
cards.quote: A founder effect is drift at the start of a population: a small group carries, by chance, a different set of alleles than the population it left.
cards.section: Drift and founders: chance in small populations

cards.front: In a founder population, 60 of 3,000 sampled people carry one copy of a variant and none carries two. What is the variant's allele frequency?
cards.back: 60 variant copies out of 2 x 3,000 = 6,000 allele copies, so 0.01. The carrier frequency is 1 in 50, not the allele frequency.
cards.quote: a carrier frequency of 1 in 45 is not an allele frequency of 1/45.
cards.section: Drift and founders: chance in small populations

cards.front: Founder-effect variants such as those in Tay-Sachs or Amish populations are features of what, and why is this not a statement about races?
cards.back: Of particular populations and their histories. Most human genetic variation lies within populations, not between them.
cards.quote: These are features of particular populations and their histories, not of races: most human genetic variation lies within populations, not between them.
cards.section: Drift and founders: chance in small populations

cards.front: What change does the sickle allele of HBB cause in the beta chain, and what does deoxygenated HbS do?
cards.back: Glutamate to valine at position 6 of the beta chain. Deoxygenated HbS polymerises. Sickle-cell disease (SS) is autosomal recessive.
cards.quote: changes glutamate to valine at position 6 of the β chain, and deoxygenated HbS polymerises
cards.section: Balanced polymorphism: sickle cell and malaria

cards.front: In a malaria region, AS survives better than both AA and SS. Should S disappear, become fixed, or settle between? Why?
cards.back: It settles between. Rare S sits mostly in favoured AS, while common S makes more SS, which selection removes: heterozygote advantage.
cards.quote: Between the extremes: rare S sits mostly in favoured AS, while common S makes more SS, which selection removes.
cards.section: Balanced polymorphism: sickle cell and malaria

cards.front: In Kenyan coast children, sickle-cell trait (AS) did not change asymptomatic parasite carriage. How did protection vary with malaria severity?
cards.back: Protection grew with severity: about 50% against mild malaria, 75% against hospital admission and almost 90% against severe disease. That supports heterozygote advantage.
cards.quote: it was associated with about 50% protection against mild malaria, 75% against hospital admission and almost 90% against severe disease.
cards.section: Balanced polymorphism: sickle cell and malaria

cards.front: Relative survival is 0.80 for AA, 1.00 for AS, 0.40 for SS. With survival the only force, random mating and a large population, where does S settle? Use q = s/(s + t), costs s to AA and t to SS.
cards.quote: The allele settles where the losses at the two homozygotes balance
cards.section: Balanced polymorphism: sickle cell and malaria

cards.front: Illustrative data: newborns AA 0.64, AS 0.32, SS 0.04 (q = 0.2). Survival to adulthood is AA 0.90, AS 1.00, SS 0.50. Predict adult genotype frequencies and compare adult heterozygotes with Hardy-Weinberg for the adult q.
cards.back: Survivors 0.576, 0.32, 0.02 of 0.916: adults AA 0.629, AS 0.349, SS 0.022. Adult q = 0.197 predicts 0.316 heterozygotes, so adults show an excess. Newborns fit; adults do not, so sampling time matters.
cards.quote: Adults show a heterozygote excess, even though their newborns fit.

cards.front: Two populations, each at Hardy-Weinberg with different S frequencies, are pooled in one adult sample. Would the sample show a heterozygote excess or deficit? How could that separate migration from selection?
cards.back: A deficit. Selection in malarious regions predicts an excess, so a deficit favours mixing, unless migrants were themselves selected. Record where each adult was born.
cards.quote: the mixture shows a heterozygote deficit, not an excess, unless the adult migrants were themselves selected in a malarious region

cards.front: A small isolated population has a rare recessive allele at q = 0.02 after a founder effect, and relatives often mate. Will affected births be more or fewer than 1 in 2,500?
cards.back: More. Inbreeding puts more copies of the rare recessive allele into aa people without changing q. It rests on non-random mating changing genotype frequencies only.
cards.quote: By putting more rare recessive copies into aa individuals, they can still expose those alleles to selection.

cards.front: Malaria is eliminated, so AA and AS survive equally, but SS still dies young. How should the S frequency change, and how fast?
cards.back: When S is rare, S declines slowly. Selection acts only on SS, and most S copies are hidden in AS carriers. The rule is that selection against a rare recessive is slow.
cards.quote: Against a rare recessive it is slow, because selection acts only on aa, and almost every a copy is hidden in a carrier.
